title: Next wins key appeal to overturn £30m equal pay ruling
description: Next has won an appeal allowing it to keep paying warehouse workers a higher hourly rate than shop floor staff in a long running battle over equal pay
body: Next has won an appeal allowing it to keep paying warehouse workers a higher hourly rate than shop floor staff in a long running battle over equal pay.The Employment Appeal Tribunal has overturned a key part of a landmark ruling in 2024 which found the retailer was wrong to pay its warehouse staff higher basic pay than shop floor workers for jobs of equal value.More than 3,500 current and former employees, mainly women, had been set to share potentially more than £30m in back pay as a result of that judgement.After Next's appeal, the law firm Leigh Day, which represents store workers, described the conclusion on basic pay as "disappointing" and said it will appeal the decision.The tribunal accepted that Next was justified in paying higher rates because of recruitment and retention pressures for warehouse workers.Next described the decision as a "landmark victory" succeeding on the "key issue of basic pay".In a statement, it said: "The importance of this decision is that the Appeal Tribunal has confirmed that it was justifiable for Next to rely on market forces to distinguish between different groups of employees, where there was a good rationale to pay one group more than the other."In this case, Next had to pay a higher market rate to warehouse operatives because of recruitment and retention pressures, which did not apply to the workforce in its stores. Next believes this element of the judgment is not only correct in law, but also a victory for common sense."The judgment affirms a principle at the heart of any effective employment market - that employers must be able to pay what is necessary to recruit the people they need; and that doing so does not oblige them to raise the pay of other employees where there is no reason to do so."Leigh Day said judges did uphold 2024 findings on night-time premiums, overtime premiums and paid rest breaks.Next said it will now seek permission to appeal these decisions.Both the original Employment Tribunal and the Appeal Tribunal found there was no direct sex discrimination in Next's pay rates. Shop floor staff are predominantly women while warehouse workers are predominantly male.Last year, thousands of female workers at Birmingham City Council heard how much money they will receive in a long-awaited equal pay settlement. Brighton and Hove City Council is also facing over 1,000 equal pay cases.

schema.headline: Next wins key appeal to overturn £30m equal pay ruling

title: Plans for major overhaul of councils halted
description: Plans for a major shake-up of local government are on hold, after the government launched a review in light of new legal advice.Proposals to merge sma
body: Plans for a major shake-up of local government are on hold, after the government launched a review in light of new legal advice.Proposals to merge smaller councils to form larger authorities in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk have been withdrawn.Meanwhile, plans for 14 other areas will also be reviewed and paused.Reorganisation in Surrey, where councillors for two new unitary authorities were elected in May, will not be affected by the review.The government confirmed local elections in May 2027 would go ahead on existing council boundaries.Confirming the review in Parliament, Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner told MPs that "in light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law".She added: "And secondly, I want to fully test whether our proposals for local government reorganisation meet the priorities of a new administration and a new prime minister and any additional considerations."Rayner acknowledged the announcement was "disappointing" but insisted the government was "determined more than ever to devolve power closer to the people we represent" - a key priority of new PM Andy Burnham.The plans originated under Sir Keir Starmer's government, when Rayner was also local government secretary, before she was replaced by Steve Reed.The government was already facing legal challenges over proposals to reorganise councils in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.In June, Reform-led councils in Essex, Norfolk and Suffolk launched judicial reviews against the plans, while the Conservative-led administration in Hampshire did the same.Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "Reform UK not only argued that this government's plans for local government reorganisation were an unmitigated disaster, but we once again put our money where our mouth is."He added: "Thanks to our judicial reviews in affected Reform-led councils, the government has backed down on their plans yet again."Conservative shadow local government minister David Simmonds said it was a "humiliation" for the government. He said: "Ministers are only backing off because they have been found out in the face of relentless Conservative opposition to their gerrymandering."Liberal Democrat local government spokeswoman Zöe Franklin said: "This is an embarrassing and chaotic climbdown, which has resulted in already cash-strapped councils wasting huge sums on plans the government told them were legally watertight."Sean Matthews, from the County Councils Network, welcomed the move, adding: "Many of our members will be relieved that the decisions they viewed as damaging to local services and financially unsustainable have been withdrawn or are being reviewed."A spokesperson for the Local Government Association, which represents councils, said that while local authorities hold different views on the reorganisation plans "there is no excuse for the government's mishandling of this process".The spokesperson added that Rayner's announcement "will have caused significant uncertainty, after councils have invested scarce public money and countless hours" in the reorganisation programme.Local government in England is currently covered by a complicated patchwork of arrangements.In some places, responsibility for local services is shared between county councils, which manage areas including social care and education; and district councils, which cover smaller areas and are responsible for services such as bin collections.Some areas, particularly larger towns and some cities, have "unitary" authorities responsible for both - while the regions surrounding big cities are increasingly covered by regional mayors and multi-council "combined" authorities, with greater powers in areas such as transport policy, planning and housing.In late 2024, as local government secretary, Rayner announced plans to move towards unitary councils across all of England, with council boundaries redrawn and smaller district councils abolished.The government argued the proposals would make the system simpler and produce savings by making the delivery of services more efficient, while also handing new powers from Westminster to regions across the country.However, critics said the plans would not save money, while diverting resources from front-line services and leaving councils more remote from their communities.Under Sir Keir, the government had been pushing ahead with the proposals.In July – just days before Burnham became prime minister – Rayner's successor as secretary of state, Reed, had announced plans for new councils in 14 areas.

schema.headline: Plans for major overhaul of councils halted

title: New Inbetweeners film confirmed by Netflix as lead stars return
description: Ooh, sequel friend! A new Inbetweeners movie is officially in the works, Netflix has confirmed. The original cast of Simon Bird, James Buckley, Blake
body: Ooh, sequel friend! A new Inbetweeners movie is officially in the works, Netflix has confirmed. The original cast of Simon Bird, James Buckley, Blake Harrison and Joe Thomas will reprise their roles for the feature film, with production starting on Monday.The Inbetweeners 3 will follow on the story of their characters, Will McKenzie, Jay Cartwright, Neil Sutherland and Simon Cooper.They originally starred in three seasons of the popular coming-of-age sitcom, which aired on E4 between 2008 and 2010.It followed their trials and misadventures as suburban teenagers at the fictional Rudge Park Comprehensive as they navigated school life and friendship.The show has gained new fans over the years due to some of its best bits finding new life on social media, as well as through the film sequels.The third instalment follows two sequels backed by Film4, which were released in 2011 and 2014. Alongside the announcement, Netflix released a teaser video which showed Will, Simon, Neil and Jay return to their iconic yellow Fiat. The friend group all get into the tiny car but Simon struggles to start the engine. After some encouragement, it gets going and they drive out of what looks like a storage unit. Production kicks off after months of speculation that there would be another film, but beyond the lead characters returning, the rest of the cast is yet to be confirmed. Fans will be wondering if English actress Emily Atack will return in her role as Charlotte Hinchcliffe, or if Emily Head will come back as Carli D'Amato.However, Netflix has announced The Inbetweeners creators, Damon Beesley and Iain Morris, will return to write and direct the film.Beesley and Morris said it has been "super fun" hanging out with friends again. "We're going to work hard every week to ensure there are no problemos making this new film for humans," they added. The first film sees the group of friends head to Crete in Greece for a post sixth form break, but they quickly find more trouble than they bargained for. The 2014 follow-up reunites Will, Simon, and Neil as they travel to Australia to visit Jay during his gap year - where they find out his travels aren't as lavish as his messages had claimed.Tensions rise as they clash over whether to chase cultural experiences or a wilder time on their trip.  The first film made history as the biggest opening weekend for a UK comedy at the time, according to Netflix, while the sequel also broke box office records.

schema.headline: New Inbetweeners film confirmed by Netflix as lead stars return

title: Grindr to pay £26m to settle claims it allegedly shared users' HIV status
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByLiv McMahonTechnology reporterGrindr has agreed to pay £26m to settle a lawsuit over allegations it shared users' personal
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByLiv McMahonTechnology reporterGrindr has agreed to pay £26m to settle a lawsuit over allegations it shared users' personal information - including their HIV status - with third parties.The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app was sued in the High Court in 2024 over claims it misused people's personal information.The class action suit was later served in the US, with the law firm leading the case saying it had signed up more than 11,000 claimants.According to a US regulatory filing, Grindr will make two £13m payments to settle the claims. The firm said the settlement includes no admission of liability.Grindr stressed the claims relate to "historical data practices" before 2020 when it was owned by Chinese firm Kunlun.The filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, external by Grindr said a settlement had been reached on 2 September."While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognizes and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period," the company said in its filing.The firm has agreed to pay £13m to the counterparties by 31 December and a further £13m by 31 March 2027.'Significant distress'The claims brought more than two years ago by law firm Austen Hayes alleged Grindr had shared sensitive data with third parties for commercial purposes, breaching UK privacy laws.It said this included information about the ethnicity and sexual orientation of its users.People on Grindr have the option to share their HIV status along with when they were last tested - a move it says aims to reduce stigma, facilitate conversations and help users make informed health choices.Chaya Hanoomanjee, the lawyer who led the claim, said in April 2024 claimants had "experienced significant distress" over their sensitive and private information being shared without their consent.She said the company "owes it to the LGBTQ+ community it serves to compensate those whose data has been compromised".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Grindr became a publicly-listed company in 2022, two years after it was taken over by new ownersTwo data analytics services, Apptimize and Localytics, were identified as third parties with access to the sensitive data.The claim said a potentially unlimited number of third parties used it to customise advertisements to Grindr's users.It followed revelations in 2018 that Grindr had been sharing personal data, including the HIV status of its users, with the two data analytics providers.Grindr defended the practice at the time as in line with industry standards – but it said it then stopped sharing HIV data with those companies.It was fined £5.5m by Norway's data protection watchdog and, later in 2022, reprimanded by the UK Information Commissioner's Office for its data practices.The company said in its filing on Friday that since 2020, it had "overhauled" its privacy practices to help meet the "unique needs of its community"."Grindr is and remains a safe space for users, committed to transparency, user control, and responsible data practices," it said.

schema.headline: Grindr to pay £26m to settle claims it allegedly shared users' HIV status

title: Prince Harry and Meghan not working royals, says King
description: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex will not be working royals allowed to carry out official engagements now they have returned to the UK, a letter sent on
body: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex will not be working royals allowed to carry out official engagements now they have returned to the UK, a letter sent on behalf of King Charles spells out.The letter is intended to clarify the status of Prince Harry and Meghan, who moved back from California with children Archie and Lilibet last month.They will still not be able to use the "HRH" titles of His and Her Royal Highness, and remain "private citizens", says the letter sent on behalf of the King by the Lord Chamberlain, a top Palace official.It has been sent to Prince Harry's team, government departments, military officials and Lord Lieutenants, according to Palace sources.Lord Lieutenants, who are the monarch's local representatives, and government staff are often involved in royal visits and engagements.This letter makes clear that any engagements carried out by the Sussexes will be in a private capacity and they will not be representing the Royal Family.It seems to be something of a shot across the bows, making clear that any Prince Harry and Meghan visits should not be treated as royal engagements.This comes ahead of what are likely to be public appearances by the Sussexes this autumn, as they settle in the UK and support their charities.The message from the King emphasises that the position agreed in 2020 when the Sussexes left the UK - the so-called Sandringham Agreement - is still in place.This ruled out any "half-in and half-out" status, so Harry and Meghan could not pursue their own commercial interests while continuing to be working royals."It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of the Sovereign, and are no longer working members of the Royal Family," the letter says.The letter sent on behalf of the King makes it clear that this remains the case."The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity," it adds.The King's message says that any questions from organisations about the reception to be given to the Sussexes, "particularly where recourse to public funds may be required, should be directed to Buckingham Palace".Prince Harry and Meghan faced an acrimonious departure from the UK in 2020, which they chronicled in their Netflix documentary.They established their financial independence in California, including Prince Harry writing a best-selling memoir Spare and Meghan creating an online food range, As Ever.This summer the couple made a surprise return to the UK, where their children will be going to school.It's expected that Prince Harry will be supporting his charities, including the Invictus Games, which are due to be held in Birmingham next year.There have been reports that Meghan is considering a return to acting.Disputes about Prince Harry and Meghan's security in the UK remain unresolved and the letter spells out: "Any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities."Prince Harry has complained about a lack of adequate police protection in the UK, but the Palace says that has to be addressed by the Royal and VIP Executive Committee - known as Ravec - which decides security for royals and public figures.Palace sources have suggested it was better to make the Lord Chamberlain's letter public, in a spirit of transparency, rather than risk it emerging in leaks.Prince Harry and Meghan's representatives have been contacted for a response.

schema.headline: Prince Harry and Meghan not working royals, says King

title: Liverpool transfers: Busy in-tray for next sporting director
description: Who will be new Liverpool sporting director - and what issues do they face?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Michael Edwards (centre) and Richa
body: Who will be new Liverpool sporting director - and what issues do they face?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Michael Edwards (centre) and Richard Hughes (centre-right) have both left Liverpool this summer.ByFootball reporterWith Richard Hughes' move to Al-Hilal now confirmed, Liverpool are seeking a new sporting director for the fifth time since 2022.Hughes joined Liverpool in the summer of 2024 and oversaw the appointments of Arne Slot then Andoni Iraola. He informed the club earlier this year that he wanted to pursue a new challenge in Saudi Arabia.Mike Gordon, the president of Fenway Sports Group (FSG), is overseeing the process of finding Hughes' replacement, with Liverpool keen to make a swift appointment. Liverpool will look at internal candidates, but have not ruled out the possibility of appointing someone from outside the club. There is a desire to have someone that is committed long term.But who are candidates? And what challenges do they face?Who are the candidates?David Woodfine, who was Hughes' assistant and was previously Liverpool's director of loans is one potential candidate. Woodfine was pictured giving Iraola a tour of the facilities at the AXA Training Centre when he arrived in June.Another is Julian Ward, who was Liverpool's sporting director between 2022 and 2023 and oversaw the signings of Luis Diaz, Cody Gakpo, Alexis Mac Allister and Darwin Nunez. He is now FSG's technical director.Pedro Marques is FSG's director of football development and was previously the technical director at Benfica, where he helped sign Enzo Fernandez for £10m and before that, a first-team performance analyst at Manchester City. Outside Anfield, Luis Campos at Paris St-Germain would be the strongest appointment but he is unlikely to view his immediate future away from the European champions. Whoever replaces Hughes - who has also taken two members of Liverpool's recruitment staff in Mark Burchill and Craig McKee to the Middle East - they will have plenty to address. Do Liverpool try to keep Alisson and Van Dijk?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Van Dijk and Alisson both joined Liverpool in 2018Alisson's deal expires at the end of the season and although Juventus were interested in the Brazil goalkeeper this summer, Liverpool had no intention of letting him leave.Iraola appointed Alisson one of his vice-captains and the 33-year-old has started in all three of their league games so far. He remains comfortably their best goalkeeper even if he is not at his peak.Liverpool are not short of options, although Giorgi Mamardashvili has not fully convinced thus far while 18-year-old Lucca Brughmans will arrive next summer from Genk in a deal worth up to £30m but is unlikely to be viewed as an immediate first choice.Alisson has been one of Liverpool's best players during a period in which they won two Premier League titles and a Champions League and the new sporting director will have to decide whether to try and keep him at Anfield next season. The same can be said of skipper Virgil van Dijk, who is out of contract next summer. Having lost senior figures Mohamed Salah and Andy Robertson at the end of last season, Liverpool need experience, so losing both Alisson and Van Dijk in the same close season would carry risk.After an extended break following the World Cup, the 35-year-old has played every minute of Liverpool's league campaign so far and although he may not be quite the force he once was, he is still comfortably one of Europe's best centre-backs.Jeremy Jacquet, Giovanni Leoni, Ifeanyi Ndukwe and Mor Talla Ndiaye have huge potential and the new sporting director may view Van Dijk as the perfect player for them to learn from.What about Liverpool's midfield and attack?Iraola believes Liverpool have "good numbers" in midfield despite not strengthening that position over the summer following Curtis Jones' move to Inter Milan.Faith has been placed in Trey Nyoni to feature more this season and the 19-year-old was one of the standouts of Liverpool's pre-season tour of the USA. As the fixture list heats up, a lot will be asked of Dominik Szoboszlai, Ryan Gravenberch and Mac Allister, so an injury to any of them could prove a major issue.As reported last week by BBC Sport, Liverpool have looked at Monaco's Lamine Camara but were not open to buying a midfielder this summer.That position could become a priority in January or next summer, particularly if it looks likely that there will be no contract extension for Mac Allister, whose deal expires in 2028.As things stand, there are no talks over a new deal for the Argentina midfielder. That will be another situation for Hughes' successor to pick up. The area where there is less concern is up front, with Hughes signing Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Hugo Ekitike, Victor Munoz and Bradley Barcola on his watch.With 18-year-old Rio Ngumoha expected to sign a long-term deal, Liverpool appear well-stocked in that department. Liverpool eventually decided not to allow Cody Gakpo to leave for Manchester City this summer. The Netherlands forward has one goal and three assists already this season, but if they were able to sign a new winger and received another lucrative bid for Gakpo, that could be a scenario the club revisit.Building a relationship with IraolaWhen the question of stability was put to Billy Hogan, Liverpool's CEO, this summer, he told BBC Sport: "I would send a message that we are in a very healthy place as a football club - the leadership from the ownership is in a very steady place and we're looking forward to the next season and the season ahead."However this has been a summer where Liverpool have changed managers, welcomed new investors, lost a number of senior players and seen their sporting director leave a year earlier than expected. Michael Edwards, who appointed Hughes, also resigned as FSG's CEO of Football.Hughes, who is understood to have been influenced by Edwards' departure, was integral in the decision to sack Slot and appoint Iraola and ultimately the new sporting director will have a big say in the Spaniard's future.When he joined Liverpool, Iraola said he only signed a two-year-deal because he didn't just want to be somewhere because he had a contract.His relationship with Hughes from their time at Bournemouth played a part in him getting the Liverpool job. Now it will be down to someone else to work in tandem with Iraola as Liverpool look to challenge again.

schema.headline: Liverpool transfers: Busy in-tray for next sporting director

title: Europe wrestles with impact of historic regional gains for Germany’s AfD
description: "Seismic", "a socio-political earthquake", "a watershed moment for Germany".This was how political analysts and many media outlets described the stunn
body: "Seismic", "a socio-political earthquake", "a watershed moment for Germany".This was how political analysts and many media outlets described the stunning victory of the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in local elections in Germany on Sunday. Is that an exaggeration?Saxony-Anhalt is one of the smallest of massive Germany's 16 regions. It boasts a mere 1.7 million out of 59 million eligible voters nationwide. How significant can its political sentiments be, especially since the AfD narrowly failed to win an outright majority?The answer: Very significant.First and foremost, at home in Germany.The vote may have been regional but it impacts at national level. The AfD landslide piles even more pressure on the already beleaguered centrist coalition government in Berlin. It may prove to be the nail in the political coffin of Germany's deeply unpopular conservative Chancellor, Friedrich Merz. He had promised to slash the AfD's popularity.These political woes will further weaken and distract Germany, the EU's most powerful player, at a time of continental crisis - as Europe struggles to contain Russian aggression, US President Donald Trump's tariff tantrums and the economic threat from China.The Saxony-Anhalt result also provokes soul-searching throughout Germany, where the Nazi past still looms large. This is the first outstanding electoral landslide for a hard-right nationalist party - giving it a real shot at governing, in this case, at regional level - since the fall of the Third Reich in 1945.The German authorities have labelled the AfD, in part, anti-democratic and a number of regional factions of the party, including Saxony-Anhalt, far-right extremist.The AfD is well-known to be particularly popular in east Germany but it is now also polling as the biggest political party nationwide.Germany's political mainstream has failed voters, it would seem. What does Europe's biggest single economy, its most populous nation not counting Russia, do now?Tiny Saxony-Anhalt is causing waves outside Germany, too.None other than the US president swiftly posted the Saxony-Anhalt exit poll on his Truth Social platform on Sunday.The AfD's anti-immigration, anti-woke, "Germany for Germans" message chimes closely with Donald Trump's Maga [Make America Great Again] missive. Along with a number of other nationalist parties in Europe, the AfD borrows heavily from the Trump playbook - undermining mainstream media, questioning the neutrality of judges and promising to "make Germany great again".Interesting to note though - the US president is rarely name-checked on the campaign trail in Europe. Politicians are keenly aware just how unpopular he is amongst voters.Hot on Donald Trump's social media heels on Sunday night was the influential Russian businessman Kirill Dmitriev, CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund. He declared the AfD result "historic", Germany's national government "discredited" and the German chancellor "humiliated", comparing Friedrich Merz to the UK's not-long-gone Prime Minister, Keir Starmer, who felt forced to resign this summer.Also watching the Saxony-Anhalt election closely was the European Union. The next 12 months is bumper election season across the EU. Ballots are expected in key nations France, Italy, Spain and Poland. Brussels fears more "extreme" parties, left but particularly right of the political spectrum, may benefit across the board.The leader of Spain's nationalist Vox party, Santiago Abascal, posted on X on Sunday that the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt was " a great hope for Germany and for Europe".By contrast, France's Europe Minister, Benjamin Haddad, an ally of centrist President Emmanuel Macron, warned "this is a serious moment in Europe, seeing the far-right win in a regional election in Germany".Neither the AfD, nor other European parties labelled "extreme right" or "hard right", accept the label. They also differ from one another in tone and party programme. France's National Rally under Marine Le Pen kicked the AfD out of its grouping in the European Parliament two years ago, for being too "radical". What the parties do tend to share, however, is an anti-immigration platform and strong nationalist messaging. And that really worries the EU.Whether it is a rallying cry for "Germany First" or "Italy First" or "France for the French!", the concern in Brussels is that the rise of nationalist parties strains European cohesion at a time when outside events demand it more than ever.Nationalist parties like the AfD or Italy's League Party tend to be deeply Eurosceptic, but Brussels says Europe needs to stand united to counter Donald Trump's bullying, for example, or to effectively protect European business against China's goods dumping.Europe's defence establishment also warns that fractures in European sanctions against Russia or countries going tepid on Nato membership (as you see in Marine Le Pen's National Rally for example, or Germany's AfD) just emboldens Moscow.Security chiefs say nations must stick together to stop Russia in Ukraine, otherwise the Kremlin will be tempted to attack inside Nato, such as the Baltic states.The thing is, Europe's voters are very aware of these outside threats and the impact they have at home. They worry about the impact of wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, about crumbling health services at home and dwindling economic security for themselves and their families. Uncontrolled immigration and safety on the streets are huge concerns, too.And this is where the significance of the Saxony-Anhalt vote shines bright - a flashing red warning to traditional political parties, but also to institutions across Europe like the judiciary and security services. Those the AfD dismisses as the self-interested "Establishment".Voters on this continent feel lost and let down by parties they have supported over and again for decades. Looking right or left now at election time does not mean they have all suddenly become extremist.The AfD campaign slogan in Saxony-Anhalt was an upbeat "Anything is Possible!" - plus a promise to make Germans feel proud of their country again. Till now untried and untested in government, people seem increasingly willing to give them a go.

schema.headline: Europe wrestles with impact of historic regional gains for Germany’s AfD

title: Self-described 'racist monster' Thomas Webster jailed after BBC investigation
description: The HMRC said it took breaches of its standards "extremely seriously" and had "robust processes" in place to investigate concerns."Where standards are
body: The HMRC said it took breaches of its standards "extremely seriously" and had "robust processes" in place to investigate concerns."Where standards are not met, we act decisively," HMRC said in a statement."Following an internal disciplinary process, the individual concerned was dismissed from HMRC and ceased to be employed by the department in February 2025."Talking to an undercover BBC reporter, Webster self-identified as a "white totalitarianist" who believed in "a world where white becomes the default human race... all other races will be extinct."Describing himself as "a guy who seeks trouble" while on a hike with other Patriotic Alternative members, he boasted that he would have "crushed [the] skulls" of a group of non-white men if they had walked near to him.Following the BBC programme, police opened an investigation and linked Webster to several social media accounts, mainly on X.He was arrested for inciting racial hatred in September 2025 and police used details on his phone and computer to confirm the accounts were his. He was charged in July and pleaded guilty last month.A number of the offending posts were still visible on X in the weeks after Webster pleaded guilty, as well as dozens of others in which he used the most extreme racist language.In these additional posts, which did not form part of the charges, Webster praised Adolf Hitler and the Nazis and told several prominent politicians that they should be killed or subjected to sexual violence.In one of his X posts, Webster described himself as a "genocidal racist monster."He described his wishes for people of several races to be killed and in one post said "the next Hitler will be a man like me!"After BBC contacted X about the posts, they were taken down - but the company did not comment further.Days before Webster's sentencing, BBC News found another active Substack account appearing to belong to him.The account shared posts discussing Webster's arrest, as well as intimate details of his personal life.It also included several comments about race, including one calling for the "total genetic extinction" of people from South Asia.One comment claimed that these posts were made in spite of bail conditions heavily limiting Webster's internet use and explicitly preventing him from communicating via social media.After the BBC contacted Substack about the content, most of the posts were taken down, although one for which Webster was charged is still visible. The company did not respond further.Warwick Crown Court heard Webster had been referred four times to the UK Government-led Prevent programme, a scheme aimed to stop people becoming terrorists. The court also heard police found a crossbow in the attic of his property, which was still in its wrapping.Jamie Scott, prosecuting, told the court that the CPS took a "proportionate approach" to charging him with 12 offences - but asked it be noted that there was "a raft" of similar material posted online by Webster.His defence lawyer Susan Guest said Webster had a long-standing difficulty around social interaction and anxiety and said he became "more isolated" where his views were "reinforced rather than challenged" by people online."He almost lived in a bubble and this online community reinforced his views," Guest told the court."That bubble subsequently popped and he now has to take responsibility for those actions."Sentencing Webster to two years, Judge Anthony Potter said he had been given numerous opportunities to show remorse and change his behaviour."Talk is very very cheap," he told Webster. "It has allowed you to escalate your offending and propagate the most harmful views."I cannot accept that there is a realistic prospect of rehabilitation in the community. I'd be failing in my public duty if I didn't sent you to custody."Frank Ferguson, the Chief Crown Prosecutor for the CPS, said inciting racial hatred was a "very serious offence" which went "beyond any debate about freedom of speech.""Expressing a wish for people to be killed… Jewish people, Muslim people, black people, south-asian people, immigrants and LGBTQ+ community as well… and encouraging other people to express similar views."It's not just about what he might do, it's what he might be encouraging others to do by his words," he said.Det Ch Supt Alison Hurst, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing for the West Midlands, said Webster had been investigated previously for racially aggravated offences and thanked BBC Wales for bringing him to their attention again."Parts of the evidence from that documentary has been presented to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which has led to the prosecution and sentencing," she said.Webster was given a two-year sentence, where he'll serve half in prison and a year on licence.If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Self-described 'racist monster' Thomas Webster jailed after BBC investigation

title: Germany's AfD calls for parties to work with it after Saxony-Anhalt win
description: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is "very, very close" to taking power in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, its deputy parliamentary lead
body: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is "very, very close" to taking power in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, its deputy parliamentary leader has told the BBC, after a historic victory in elections there.  Sunday's preliminary results show it fell three seats short of an outright majority, with 43.8% of the vote. It is now seeking support from other parties or individuals in order to govern.While most German political parties refuse to work with the AfD, Beatrix von Storch called for its opponents to enter talks and said: "You cannot say, I do not accept the vote of the people". Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he was "deeply shocked" by the result, describing it as "seismic... not just in the country but also in my own political party and I take that very seriously".His party, the conservative CDU, saw its share of the vote almost halved to 17.2% in the state's preliminary results.Merz said it was not possible to return to "business as usual", adding that the country needed "profound reforms" and the CDU needed to "reach people at an emotional level". No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing and local education.Von Storch said the state's results "were on the table and now democrats have to talk to [one] another. This is what democracy demands".She added that if parties refused to work with the AfD, "then we might end up in severe chaos and maybe we have a new election".Her comments were echoed by AfD's leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, who told a news conference on Monday that the party had won a "clear mandate to govern".The state's defeated premier, the CDU's Sven Schulze, also said the mandate to govern Saxony-Anhalt "now lies with the AfD".Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35.The party's plans for Saxony-Anhalt, which include segregating child refugees into special classes and setting up a task-force to help detain and deport migrants who no longer have the right to be in the state, are highly controversial within Germany.The AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament instead of the 42 needed for an outright majority, although the result has not yet been finalised.Von Storch told the BBC the AfD was talking to individuals within the CDU group - the largest party in both the state's outgoing coalition and Germany's government - because they were "very, very unhappy with their own party".One idea being floated is an informal deal whereby a small party - the BSW - could give their tacit support to allow the AfD to form a minority government.The left-wing populist BSW, which is set to win five seats, is also tough on immigration and backs importing Russian gas.Siegmund said discussions with other parties were initiated on Sunday night and could potentially take days or weeks to conclude. "We reach out to everybody first, we will have consultations and then we'll see whether [there are] individual parliamentary groups or MPs who would be willing to help us," he added.Another possibility - at least in theory - is a messy, minority coalition government led by the conservative CDU party. But that appears very unlikely.There's also the prospect of another election to break the deadlock - an idea which has been mooted by Siegmund who has said he doesn't want to compromise on his policy goals.The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states. They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power.Merz described the Saxony-Anhalt defeat as the worst the CDU had suffered "in years, if not decades", acknowledging that the results in upcoming regional elections in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania and Berlin could have "increasing significance".Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally. Commentators and political opponents called AfD's victory a watershed and break with the past. "This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," Siegmund told supporters overnight. "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal."On Sunday, US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the state's projected results on his Truth Social platform. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev then took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD".Dmitriev had earlier praised the Russia-friendly AfD as "the party of hope and reason, co-operation truth and hope for Germany". Ahead of Germany's federal election last year, US Vice-President JD Vance endorsed the party, in a move criticised in Germany as political interference.Polish centre-right Prime Minister Donald Tusk saw the result very differently, saying "in Poland only idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD".Asked about those who had expressed fears over the far-right party gaining power in the state, deputy parliamentary leader Beatrix von Storch told the BBC that its supporters were afraid of "losing our economy, they are afraid of losing our inner security".She said conservative voters were turning to alternative political parties because they were not being listened to.She added that the party's detractors should: "Wake up and realise what happened in several other European states... The conservative parties will disappear from the landscape as it happened in Italy, as it's about to happen in the UK, as it might also happen in France".

schema.headline: Germany's AfD calls for parties to work with it after Saxony-Anhalt win

title: Thousands turn out in Serbia for funeral of  'Butcher of Bosnia' Ratko Mladić
description: Thousands of people have turned out in Serbia's capital, Belgrade, to attend the funeral of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić. Widely known as t
body: Thousands of people have turned out in Serbia's capital, Belgrade, to attend the funeral of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić. Widely known as the Butcher of Bosnia, Mladić died at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence in the UN prison in The Hague, the Netherlands.He was found guilty of genocide by a UN war crimes tribunal for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when around 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed. It was described as Europe's worst atrocity since World War Two.A Serbian government minister had initially said that Mladić would be given a state funeral ​but those plans were changed after objections from some European leaders. On Monday, the EU denounced Mladić's "glorification". Ratko Mladić commanded Bosnian Serb forces in the 1990s against the Bosnian Croat and Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) armies.During the 1992-1995 Bosnian war, his troops committed what became known as "ethnic cleansing" in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a bid to expel the non-Serbian population by force. They besieged the capital city of Sarajevo, with the deaths of more than 10,000 people.Mladić was arrested in 2011, 16 years after he was first indicted, and sentenced to life in prison in 2021 after a nine-year trial.Despite his conviction for genocide, Mladić remains a national figure perceived by many Serbs as a heroic defender of the nation. Many Serb nationalists see him as a hero and protector, particularly in the Bosnian Serb entity of Republika Srpska, where his death sparked vigils.Several Serbian government ministers joined the crowds paying tribute outside the church where Mladić lay in state before the burial, including the Defence Minister Bratislav Gašić, and the Minister of Justice Nenad Vujić, local media reported. The funeral service was led by the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Porfirije, who said Mladić's name would remain "deeply etched in the memory and prayers of the majority of our Serbian Orthodox people, who feel and nurture a deep sense of gratitude towards him".Early in the day, long queues formed outside the small St Luka church, as people waited to go in and pay their respects to the coffin. Many of those in the crowds were army veterans and some men were draped in flags printed with his picture on.Crowds arrived several hours before the funeral began to light candles outside the church, accompanied by a choir on a loudspeaker in the sunshine.Inside the church, Mladić's coffin was guarded by several men, mainly war veterans, while his wife, son, and grandchildren stood inside receiving condolences.In a sign of the reverence held for the former general, his coffin was flown back to Serbia last week on a government plane, and was carried from the plane by six soldiers and draped in flags.Free bus services were organised from Bosnia and most towns in Serbia for anyone who wanted to pay their respects.On Sunday night, fans of the Serbian football club Red Star Belgrade unveiled a display of Mladic before their derby win over Partizan Belgrade. For others, the funeral has rekindled painful memories of the war.A woman in Sarajevo called Zdravka Gvozdjar - whose nine-year-old son was killed by Mladić-led forces during the siege of the city - told Reuters news agency it was "really horrible" that the funeral was taking place in Belgrade. Mladić "deserved to be erased from memory for good, not to be... promoted as a hero," she said. "He should be remembered only as a butcher."Thousands attended the funeral because he "remains a figure of national pride and defiance," said Daniella Peled, Editor at the Institute of War and Peace Reporting NGO - who covered Mladić's war crimes trial in detail. The war crimes tribunal "provided an incredibly detailed historical record of Mladić's crimes," she told the BBC, but the Serbian media and education system "has not reflected the true scale of his crimes or the perspectives of victims and survivors."Pro-government Serbian media "depict him as a loyal soldier who simply carried out his duties," Peled said. "It's extremely challenging for post-conflict societies to undertake a national reckoning or acknowledge responsibility for the crimes of the past."

schema.headline: Thousands turn out in Serbia for funeral of  'Butcher of Bosnia' Ratko Mladić

title: Cancer survivors living with chemo hair loss celebrate resilience
description: Chemo hair loss doesn't define me - it's a symbol that I'm strongImage source, Caroline SikkenkImage caption, Rhiannon is one of 11 Welsh women who ha
body: Chemo hair loss doesn't define me - it's a symbol that I'm strongImage source, Caroline SikkenkImage caption, Rhiannon is one of 11 Welsh women who have been photographed for The Pink Ribbon Foundation's BOLD campaignByNicola BryanBBC WalesUpdated 7 September 2026 06:15 BSTWhen Rhiannon Thomas lost her hair during chemotherapy just weeks after having a mastectomy, her confidence was at an all time low. But being photographed for a campaign that celebrates the resilience of women living with breast cancer helped her find an inner strength she never knew she had. "For the first time I feel I look pretty, I look confident and strong," said the 36-year-old mum."It's surprising the strength you find when you go through such a hard time."Image source, Rhiannon ThomasImage caption, Rhiannon Thomas recently completed her chemotherapyRhiannon, a mother to two daughters aged 14 and nine, was diagnosed with breast cancer after finding a lump while in the shower in November 2025. "I had an absolute breakdown," said the teaching assistant."Like, how do you tell your children? I was so scared to just tell them."Since then she's had a mastectomy, chemotherapy and is currently having radiotherapy. When her hair began falling out during chemotherapy she decided to shave her head, but wanted to make it as positive an experience as possible for her children. She encouraged her youngest to play at being a hairdresser and do whatever she wanted with a scissors before getting the shaver out. "I was like, 'just cut whatever you want because it's going anyway'," said Rhiannon."I wanted to make something hard joyful for my children and for myself because I didn't want them to see me upset, and my daughter loved it."Image source, Rhiannon ThomasImage caption, When Rhiannon was diagnosed with breast cancer her first thought was her childrenFootage captured on her phone shows the family laughing at home in Abertridwr, near Caerphilly, as her daughter got creative with the scissors.But afterwards, in private moments, the radical change to her appearance was hard."I remember looking in the mirror and like just crying because it's just you know we don't recognise yourself," she said.Rhiannon was brought to tears recalling the look on her parents' faces when they first saw her after her head had been shaved. She took to wearing a head wrap whenever she left the house. Image source, Caroline SikkenkImage caption, Sam Gronow-Walters says she is proud of her portraitsAll this sounds very familiar to mental health nurse and mother-of-two Sam Gronow-Walters.The 44-year-old has also lost her hair though breast cancer treatment. Her cancer is incurable. She was first diagnosed with triple negative breast cancer, external five years ago, which was successfully treated with intravenous chemotherapy, a lumpectomy and radiotherapy, followed by oral chemotherapy.But seven months later she found another lump and tests showed it had returned.A mastectomy followed and she was told she was cancer-free. In 2024, she was told it had spread to her lung. Last July, tests showed it had spread to her liver and lymph nodes."You've got to keep going," said Sam from St Athan in the Vale of Glamorgan."You've just got to do whatever you can because I want to see my kids grow up."Image source, Caroline SikkenkImage caption, Sam was diagnosed with breast cancer five years agoLike Rhiannon, when she felt she had no option other than to shave her head, Sam's thoughts were immediately how to make it easier on her children, a daughter aged 20 and a son aged 13.  Her son requested she have her head shaved with a bit left at the front in homage to Brazilian footballer Ronaldo's memorable hairdo at  the 2002 World Cup - and she obliged."To me that that's quite a happy memory, so he'll see that even when I'm poorly I can still have fun, can still smile and I can still make my children happy and laugh," she said. Again, she was concerned about the impact her new appearance would have on her children."I used to ask my son when I took him to school, 'do you mind if I don't wear a hat?'" recalled Sam."He was like, 'why would I care?'."Image source, Sam Gronow-WaltersImage caption, Sam agreed to have her hair styled like Brazilian footballer Ronaldo's memorable hairdo in the 2002 World Cup finals Rhiannon and Sam first met after signing up to be part of breast cancer charity Pink Ribbon Foundation's BOLD Wales campaign.The project celebrates the courage and confidence of women who have lost their hair through breast cancer. Alongside nine other Welsh women they spent a day in Cardiff being photographed by Dutch photographer Caroline Sikkenk. The photos will be displayed at London's Piccadilly Lights next month.Image source, Sam Gronow-WaltersImage caption, Sam says her husband and children help her stay positiveBoth women had been nervous about being photographed but said the experience couldn't have been more joyful."It was like we'd all known each other before meeting that day, and we still keep in touch now," said Sam.Rhiannon had never spoken to another woman who had lost her hair during cancer treatment."I just felt really safe and not judged," she said.Figure caption, The beauty and resilience of women living with cancer is celebrated though photographySeeing the photos for the first time was emotional for both. "I was like, 'oh wow'," said Rhiannon, who was proud of the courage it had taken to be photographed at such a vulnerable time. Sam barely recognised herself."I was like, 'wow, that's not me'," she said."I was quite proud to show them to my family to say, 'oh, this is me'."Image caption, Rhiannon, Sam and the other women who took part in the campaign have stayed in touch after the photoshootBOLD began in 2022, when Lisa Allen from The Pink Ribbon Foundation met  photographer Caroline Sikkenk at a breast cancer conference.Caroline had spent years photographing women who had experienced hair loss through illness."What struck us about her photographs was that these women weren't being shown as patients," said Lisa. "They were strong, beautiful and completely themselves."The first BOLD shoot took place in 2023."What we hadn't anticipated was that we would create a community," said Lisa.She said the impact often began before a photograph has been taken."We set up a WhatsApp group beforehand, so by the time the women arrive they already feel they're going through it together."The friendships and support that grow around it last long after the photograph is taken."Image source, The Pink Ribbon FoundationImage caption, Lisa Allen from The Pink Ribbon Foundation, on the right pictured with Rhiannon, says a community has grown around the projectBoth women said taking part in the project had given them a new-found strength and sense of optimism."I feel like my confidence and my positivity just got stronger from the photoshoot," said Rhiannon."I walked out of there just so confident and I felt so free and like I don't have to hide."Gone are the head wraps and proudly showing her shaved head has become "the new normal".For Sam, the photoshoot helped her find self-acceptance."This is me now - I wouldn't have long hair again," she said. "Hair loss doesn't define who I am. It's just a symbol that I'm getting through this and I am strong."If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Cancer survivors living with chemo hair loss celebrate resilience

title: Cwmbran man 'pushed off pub stage' before death, inquest told
description: Man, 102, with dementia died after being pushed in pub, inquest toldA 102-year-old man with dementia who was allegedly pushed at a Cwmbran pub died ne
body: Man, 102, with dementia died after being pushed in pub, inquest toldA 102-year-old man with dementia who was allegedly pushed at a Cwmbran pub died nearly two weeks later, an inquest has heard.Philip Ormerod, from Cwmbran, Torfaen, was taken to hospital in a critical condition following an incident at the Crows Nest pub in the town on 1 August.He is understood to have been visiting the pub for a drink when he went on to a stage in the venue to complain about the volume of the music.A 56-year-old man from Llanelli, Carmarthenshire, was arrested on suspicion of inflicting grievous bodily harm, and remains on bail under investigation.The senior coroner Caroline Saunders said the former design engineer "sustained a fall at the pub", adding that it happened "following an allegation that he was pushed".The inquest heard he was taken to the Grange hospital with a fractured hip, however his condition deteriorated and he died on the 12 August.The coroner said Ormerod's death was being investigated by police and that a forensic post mortem examination had taken place.An inquest was opened but adjourned while a police investigation is carried out.The coroner said that the inquest would not be resumed if there was a criminal prosecution, however should there be a need for a conclusion, it would take place on 26 May 2027.Philip Ormerod's son Robert previously said his father was a "pub character" and that he wanted justice for him.Following Ormerod's death, Det Ch Insp Shelley Comley, senior investigating officer for Gwent Police, said a criminal investigation is ongoing and urged people to "consider the impact that inaccurate or speculative comments" including "online commentary" could have.The force is urging anyone who was at the pub between 22:00 and 23:00 BST on the night of the incident to contact them.

schema.headline: Cwmbran man 'pushed off pub stage' before death, inquest told

title: Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises
description: The chancellor may have thought about shifting the venue of his first major speech this morning.It was an absolute and total coincidence that he chose
body: The chancellor may have thought about shifting the venue of his first major speech this morning.It was an absolute and total coincidence that he chose to make it in the Coventry Manufacturing and Technology Centre (MTC), just a few minute's drive from the city's totemic HQ of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR).In the event, no one was pulling punches. The 4,000 office-based job losses at JLR were confirmed as John Healey answered questions a few miles away.Healey chose to lean into it as an example of the global turbulence against which the UK needs more resilience.The difference between this chancellor and his predecessor was he also feels that stressing fiscal discipline should instil confidence in consumers, businesses and investors, and not sap it away amid rolling fears of tax hikes.So the prime minister and his chancellor have been engaged in a conscious attempt to boost the economic vibes - "a new story", as he called it.In his speech, and in a BBC interview afterwards, this was clear. There are some positive underlying signs from consumer, business and recruiter confidence measures that indicate this message has been heard, although the hot weather and World Cup have also been factors.The Downing Street duo are trying to maintain this precious commodity of confidence and the promotion of economic animal spirits that have been suppressed by years of political and economic chaos."Borrowing costs are too high," Healey acknowledged at the start of his speech. The global rise in bond yields is like a boa constrictor squeezing the Budget maths, slowly and relentlessly, occasionally loosening its grip, but never actually slithering away entirely. It raises some reasonable questions therefore about how to balance reining in borrowing with protecting mildly better confidence?The speech did not seem to me to prepare the ground - a "pitch roll" - for significant tax rises, as I heard at the equivalent Budget "scene setters" for the past two years. "Am I right?" I asked the chancellor on this point. A pause as he sought precisely the right word formulation. "I won't comment. I can't comment. No chancellor can ahead of a Budget I will take and announce on October 28th". OK, what about the advice from one of the PM's favourite economists Lord O'Neill that the rise in borrowing rates is a golden opportunity to scrap the triple lock?This lock guarantees the state pension rising each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but some have argued it is unaffordable.  "The prime minister has said, like I have, that we must bring down welfare costs, but we are also responding to the extreme pressure that is there in wider markets," Healey said. Neither answer was a denial, but nor were they any type of confirmation. Like a stubborn batsman, the chancellor is going to stay at the crease, giving little away, in his case, about next month's Budget.There was a focus on growth. As he toured the MTC, a centre of excellence for advanced manufacturing, he said the UK's "great talent and latent potential" made it the third most innovative country in the world, and he wanted to translate that into economic growth and success in more areas.Two decades ago, Healey was responsible for the Regional Development Agencies, scrapped by the Coalition Government, that helped fund this very facility.In his speech there was a big clue about how to square the circle of investing in industrial policy at a time of tricky public finances.The "Pufins" - public finance institutions - such as the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund can invest strategically, less constrained by the government's borrowing rules. Part of the plan is Pufins to breed more unicorns ($1bn tech startups) in the UK.This is the other part of the global backdrop. Amid the tumult of trade and military wars, there is arguably one of the biggest financial events in world history.In the coming weeks, hundreds of billions of dollars will be invested and trillions in value confirmed from flotations of big American AI firms. The UK has some standout technology in this sector. The government wants to promote it.The chancellor was also, however, cautious about the impact of AI on security and on jobs. Some degree of "public control" could be required to make these changes work for everyone. It appeared a little less cheerleading than the stance of the Starmer administration.The chancellor was perhaps mindful of the army of manufacturing robots, laser welders, 3D metal printers, whirring into action around him.Long term, it will be growth that will determine whether his borrowing rules are met, he said.Ultimately he will be judged by his actual policy choices, but where there are trade-offs between balancing the books and economic growth across the country, this sounds like a chancellor who might prioritise the latter.

schema.headline: Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises

title: Dolly Parton's sister pleads for end to 'AI garbage' posts after singer's death
description: Dolly Parton's sister has issued a plea to fans over "fake AI garbage" posted on social media in the wake of the singer's death.Tributes to the late c
body: Dolly Parton's sister has issued a plea to fans over "fake AI garbage" posted on social media in the wake of the singer's death.Tributes to the late country legend have appeared online and at locations including the Country Music Hall of Fame in Nashville, after Parton died on 25 August at the age of 80.Writing on Instagram, Stella Parton thanked those who had shown "genuine support" for the star and her family - but said a "tremendous amount of AI and endless garbage being posted" had been "challenging to absorb".Her request for people to show "more compassion" in how they respond to Parton's death follows similar pleas from families of late celebrities over AI tributes.In October, Robin Williams' daughter asked fans to stop sending fake AI-generated videos of her father.Zelda Williams' plea was shared by Dr Martin Luther King Jr's daughter Bernice A King, who asked fans to "please stop" in a post on Instagram.Little over a month later, Robert Redford's daughter Amy spoke out over AI content created, external to pay tribute to the American actor following his death last September."Every human being experiences pain and loss in life and my family is no different," wrote Parton in her Instagram post on Friday, external."Sadly, because of the way our lives have been lived in front of the public, we have no choice but to be subjected to incredible pressure and insensitivity from strangers."She said there had been a tide of AI and "garbage" posts, adding: "As time passes, those who are in the business of exploiting the loss and tragedies of others on a daily basis will move onto the next stampede of endless misinformation."Parton also asked that people look to her sister's life as "an example for tolerance" and mutual respect."It's not about the most clever comments, fake AI garbage or snarky tweets," she said.Another image criticised as an AI fake, shared on Instagram and X, depicted the late country singer without any make-up or a wig.One X user described it as "incredibly weird", while another called it a "violation".On YouTube, a "heartfelt fan-made tribute by Miley Cyrus" to her godmother Dolly Parton and sung in the style of the Wrecking Ball singer has had more than 1.5 million views.It has an AI label and disclaimer in the description to say it is not an "official release by Miley Cyrus or Dolly Parton's representatives".But scores of comments have been left on the video thanking Cyrus for the "perfect tribute".Other AI-generated tributes in the style of singers Pink and Celine Dion have also been widely-viewed online.And Dolly Parton herself appeared to have been concerned about the potential impact of AI on artists.She told The Hollywood Reporter, external in 2023 that while she thought AI was "going to be great for a lot of things, like science and medicine", the idea of it replacing humans "scares me"."That's like the mark of the beast. It's like you can't remake a person," she said."I want to just leave a body of work behind. I think all this stuff can be great, used in the right way. "But not to replace voices and writings and not to replace a human being that belongs to God."

schema.headline: Dolly Parton's sister pleads for end to 'AI garbage' posts after singer's death
